opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the big reason is that the core of an agent is actually really simple. It's basically just a model running in a loop, calling tools, getting results back, and deciding what to do next. You can write that in maybe a few dozen lines of code. When you build it yourself first, you really understand what's happening at every step: what's going into the prompt, what the model is actually seeing, how the tool results come back to it.

The problem we've seen with a lot of customers is that they reach for a framework right away, and the framework adds layers of abstraction that hide the prompts and responses. Then when something goes wrong, and something always goes wrong, they have no idea why. Maybe the framework is injecting some extra instructions, or formatting the tool output in a weird way, or truncating context, and you can't see it. Debugging becomes really painful because you're fighting the abstraction instead of looking at what the model saw.

So my advice is: start with the raw API, build the simplest loop you can, and look at the actual transcripts. Put yourself in the model's shoes. Once you deeply understand the primitives, frameworks can be great. They save you boilerplate and give you nice features like tracing or parallel tool calls. But you'll use them much more effectively because you know what's going on underneath, and you'll know when the framework is helping you and when it's getting in your way.

r001.rationale: The response says frameworks can hide prompts, responses, and other model inputs, making it difficult to diagnose what went wrong.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a simple agent loop with frameworks that add layers of abstraction, and advises starting simply before adopting those layers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main reason is that frameworks hide a lot of what's actually going on, and when you're building an agent, what's actually going on is really, really simple. An agent at its core is just a loop: you call the model, the model either gives you a final answer or asks to use a tool, you run the tool, you append the result, and you call the model again. That's it. That's maybe fifty lines of code. And when people see that, there's often this moment of, "wait, that's all it is?"

The problem with starting from a framework is that you end up with all these layers of abstraction between you and the model, and you lose sight of the fact that the thing that matters most is the prompt and the tool descriptions and what context the model sees at each step. Those are the levers. When something goes wrong, which it will, you need to be able to look at exactly what went into the model and exactly what came out. If there are three layers of framework in between, that gets really hard. We've seen a lot of customers debugging an agent for days, and the actual issue was that the framework was silently rewriting their system prompt or truncating tool results in a way they didn't know about.

The other thing is that frameworks tend to push you toward complexity too early. They come with multi-agent orchestration and memory modules and planning layers, and it's tempting to use all of that. But in our experience, the most successful agents are usually the simplest ones. You should only add complexity when you can demonstrably show it improves results on your task. And you can only make that call if you actually understand what the baseline looks like, which means building it yourself first.

So the advice isn't really "never use a framework." It's more: build it from scratch once so you know what's underneath. Then, if you decide to use a framework, you'll know what it's doing for you, and you'll know when it's getting in your way. And honestly, a lot of people do that exercise and then just... keep their fifty lines, because it turns out that's all they needed.

r001.rationale: The response says framework layers make it hard to inspect exactly what went into and came out of the model, making debugging harder.

r002.rationale: It says frameworks encourage adding complexity too early through orchestration, memory, and planning features, often before they improve results.

astra-6.text:
Because the core of an agent is actually pretty simple. You call a model, give it some tools, execute the tool it asks for, and feed the result back in. You can build that loop in a surprisingly small amount of code, and doing it yourself gives you a much better understanding of what’s happening.

A framework can be useful, but it also introduces abstractions. If you start there, it can be hard to tell whether a failure comes from your prompt, the model, the tool implementation, or something the framework is doing behind the scenes. When you build it yourself, you can see exactly what context the model gets and what happens at each step.

So I’d start with the simplest thing that works. Once you’ve built that and encountered the problems yourself, you’re in a much better position to decide which abstractions actually help.

r001.rationale: It says frameworks can make failures hard to trace and that building directly lets you see the model’s context and what happens at each step, communicating how they can obscure prompts and outputs.

r002.rationale: It notes that frameworks introduce abstractions and recommends starting simply, then adopting only abstractions that actually help.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the core of an agent is actually pretty simple. You give a model some tools, let it choose a tool, execute that tool, feed the result back, and keep going until it’s done. You can build that loop in a small amount of code, and doing it yourself gives you a much better understanding of what’s happening.

The hard part is figuring out what tools the model needs, what information to put in its context, and how to tell whether it’s succeeding. A framework can obscure those decisions behind abstractions before you understand them. So I’d start with the simplest thing, see where it breaks, and then bring in a framework when you know which problems you need it to solve.

r001.rationale: It says frameworks can obscure decisions behind abstractions, but does not mention debugging or obscured prompts and outputs.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting simple and notes that frameworks can obscure decisions, but does not say they make it easy to introduce unnecessary complexity.
